Mr. Speaker, there are large numbers of tin cans held together by lead solder in our grocery stores. The poisonous lead from these cans is absorbed by the food we eat. In small amounts it can cause loss of intelligence in children.
A study of cans purchased in Canada showed non-lead soldered cans with lead levels of 17 parts per billion, but the lead-soldered cans averaged 227 parts per billion. In one case the levels for one serving for a child had three times more lead than allowed by the World Health Organization.
Not all companies use lead solder and these companies must be congratulated for their concern for the consumer, but this government cannot be congratulated. It is the job of Health and Welfare to monitor lead levels in food, but the department's regulations cover only eight products, and allowable lead levels range from 80 parts per billion to 15 parts per billion.
Experts say that these standards are 20 years out of date. When this government says the lead levels fall below the acceptable amounts, we know that they are using meaningless standards.
What will this government do to assure people like Meagan Walker and other Canadians that they are not eating food with unacceptable high levels of lead contamination? Will this government set new standards that protect the Canadian consumer from domestically produced and imported lead-soldered cans?

Mr. Speaker, the Open Skies Conference, while a good idea and successful in itself, was also a timely opportunity for ministers of NATO and Warsaw Pact countries to sit down at the same table with a common purpose and, in so doing, to prefigure the Europe of the future.
In this respect, I think it is important that the debate about German unification not be captive to the language of the cold war era now ending. We must go beyond debate about whether the new Germany will be part of NATO or whether it will be neutral. Both these ways of looking at the issue presuppose the continuation of a Europe divided into two camps.
Instead, we should be talking about a new common security system for a Europe that extends from the Atlantic to the Urals, a common security system into which NATO and the Warsaw Pact must be absorbed and joyfully disappear.
Common security in Europe must be accompanied by common security elsewhere, particularly in the Arctic, and in this Canada has a special role to play. Perhaps NORAD should also be absorbed some day soon into a common security regime that involves Canada, the United States, the U.S.S.R. and, indeed, other circumpolar nations who share the goal of a demilitarized, non-nuclear zone of peace in the Arctic.

Mr. Speaker, today on behalf of all those who knew him, I wish to pay special tribute to an extraordinary man from Riviere Heva in Abitibi, Edouard Janneteau, who died on February 11, 1990 after a long illness. His career was long and impressive, so I will mention only a few of his many contributions to the well being of his fellow workers and the community. He worked at Noranda Mines for five years, was group leader for the union, and from 1964 to 1990, was the United Metal Workers of America union representative for Abitibi, Temiscamingue and James Bay. He helped establish credit unions in Val d'Or, Rouyn-Noranda and Malartic, and one that will open shortly in Riviere Heva. He was concillor for two years and then mayor of Riviere Heva from 1985 to 1989.
Mr. Speaker, Edouard Janneteau was known as a man who listened to what people had to say and gave good advice. Personally, I will never forget the advice he gave me when I was a member of the metal workers union in Matagami and recently as a member of Parliament. I wish to offer my sincere condolences to his wife, Anita, his children and his family.

Mr. Speaker, the students of this country deserve better than they are getting from this government. First of all, the government takes away a lot of the equalization payments, thereby reducing the funding for education. Now the Minister of Employment and Immigration has said that she is going to cut the SEED program to make funding for a program to keep young people in school.
She says that the cost of providing jobs for students during the summer months has been taken over by the private sector and does not need to be financed anymore. That may be the case in Toronto, but it is cold comfort for students in Atlantic Canada. As a matter of fact, this is going to run contrary to the intention of the minister because students who find that they do not have summer jobs when they go to university are not going to stay in university.
Why is this government taking from one needy program to give to another? When is the government going to live up to its responsibility to the students of this country?

Mr. Speaker, the broad agreement for the Open Skies treaty announced yesterday by the 23 foreign ministers from the Warsaw Pact and NATO nations is truly a revolutionary achievement in international arms control.
The holding of this historic conference at Ottawa reflects the long-standing commitment to world disarmament by our nation, our Prime Minister and our Secretary of State for External Affairs. This Canadian advocacy is exemplified by such commitments as our leading role in seismic detection of underground nuclear tests.
It is singularly appropriate that our non-militaristic nation should host this landmark meeting which not only paved the way for aerial surveillance of disarmament but also provided a forum in which superpowers could achieve breakthroughs in troop reductions. This is a

week when the entire world hears good news from Ottawa.

Mr. Speaker, it is with a great deal of pride in my hometown that I stand in this place today to report to this House the decisive step taken by the city of Hamilton in reaffirming minority language rights.
Last night city council overwhelmingly re-affirmed its commitment to respecting minority language rights in Hamilton. The message is clear and echoes the words and beliefs of the commissioners of the Royal Commission on Bilingualism and Biculturalism who, in 1967, stated in relation to bilingualism: and I quote:
The history of countries with more than one language and culture shows how often rigid attitudes held by majorities have made common life difficult, if not impossible. For the majority to hold back from acts within its power or to allow events it would be able to prevent, out of respect for the minority, is not a product of weakness but a step forward in civilization.

Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court of British Columbia ruled last month that rail passenger service on Vancouver Island was a condition of B.C.'s entry into Confederation.
As a result, Vancouver Islanders have managed to defeat the government's destructive policy and to keep their passenger trains operating. Unfortunately, what the government could not do legally it is now trying to do through the back door. It has increased fares by 32 per cent, downgraded the service and has not maintained the cars to proper standards. In short, it is sabotaging the service.
Last week I filed an appeal against VIA's fare increase on Vancouver Island and my colleagues and I are asking municipalities, chambers of commerce, labour councils and individuals on the Island to support the fare appeal and to call on the federal government to change its policy.
If VIA's passenger service on Vancouver Island is properly maintained and properly marketed with appropriate schedules and fares, we on Vancouver Island will
prove to Canadians that not only can VIA reduce the need for subsidies, it may even make a profit.

Mr. Speaker, the latest attempt by the Mulroney government to fill the Prime Minister's promise of generous assistance to the Atlantic fishery would be laughable if it was not so cynical. After mismanaging the fishery into a state of collapse, the government has the audacity to come in and announce a rescue plan which will effectively close the port of Canso and cut the workforce in its fish plant by up to 70 per cent.
Where is the generous aid package promised over and over again by this Prime Minister? What about the people of Lockporte and Port Mouton who lost their plants last spring and have watched their communities slowly die while the Tory politicians from Atlantic Canada twiddle their thumbs in Ottawa?
The Deputy Prime Minister has stood in his place and bragged about the $21 billion given to western farmers over the past five years. How does that compare to the east coast fisheries? We have yet to see one red cent or one new program. So much for the Prime Minister's rhetoric for equal and generous treatment.
We may be plain folk who fish by the sea, but this government should not mistake our sincerity for stupidity, for we will continue to stand and stand together in demanding that this government come up with the programs and funds necessary to save our communities which face extinction because of this government's indifference.
Mr. Prime Minister, do the right thing, treat Atlantic Canada as an equal partner in this confederation of ours and do so today.

Mr. Speaker, this government may be on the verge of making one of the largest wildlife management decisions in the history of this country. Agriculture Canada has recently put forward an unrealistic proposal calling for the complete eradication of bison herds affected by brucellosis or tuberculosis in Wood Buffalo National Park.
While perhaps satisfying the concerns of ranchers encroaching on the park, this recommendation ignores the fact that large questions remain about the geographic occurrence of the diseases, the genetic significance of the bison and the ecological impact of such a policy of eradication.
Yet despite these important deficiencies in the Agriculture Canada proposal, this government has refused to fund research into alternative resolutions to the problem. There is almost no federal funding available to look into alternative policies such as herd control or vaccination programs. Moreover, the aboriginal peoples of the region affected have not had the opportunity to participate effectively in the environmental assessment process.
Therefore I urge the Minister of the Environment to implement a six-month extension on the public hearings looking into the issue of the Wood Buffalo National Park bison herd and further, to provide intervener funding so that all interested groups, and especially aboriginal peoples, can participate effectively in managing this important wildlife resource.

fiscal problem than we were on this side of the House on September 4, 1984.

Members of the New Democratic Party have their heads in the sand. They say: "There is no deficit problem. Ignore the fact that we have got a debt which is too high". They go on pressing, pressing, pressing to continue to increase spending.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, a few months ago, I announced that I intended to table amendments to the provisions of the Criminal Code with respect to firearms. We are faced with a very serious situation. Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
I have in my hand correspondence from the Daily Bread Food Bank, one of 11 such food banks in my riding of Parkdale-High Park.
According to this correspondence, the greater Toronto area now has more than 84,000 people turning to charitable food programs for emergency assistance each month. The executive director goes on to say that one child in seven in Metro Toronto belongs to a food bank family.
Nationally, on an annual basis, it is estimated that 1.4 million different people, including 560,000 children, use food banks.
In light of these shocking revelations does the minister not realize that it is his government's policies that are driving more and more people to use food banks on a permanent basis? What will he do to reverse this trend?
Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, I am rather pleased that the hon. gentleman has given me an opportunity to say exactly what is being done to reverse the trend.
Since his party was voted out of office, some 760,000 Canadians have escaped from poverty. That is what we are doing to reverse that trend.

Mr. Speaker, if they have escaped from poverty why are they lining up more and more for food banks? Since the minister does not even know what a food bank is, Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
He knows that his government has approximately three years left in its mandate. Can he give assurance to Canadians today that at the end of three years there will no longer be any need for food banks anywhere in Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Perrin Beatty (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, as long as there is any Canadian who lives in poverty it is unacceptable to this government.
Do something about it!

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare; Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman opposite says do something about it. Taking some three-quarters of a million Canadians out of poverty is something pretty concrete that has been done about it.
Members opposite cannot have it both ways. They attack any attempt that is made by the government to restore Canada's economic health. They pretend, on the other hand, that they are concerned about the plight of the poor.
These statistics show that we are on track. We are continuing to make progress in terms of fighting poverty. We will not stop until we have made further progress in fighting poverty in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for tourism.
Yesterday, the minister responsible for tourism criticized the Leader of the Opposition because he cited American tour organizers' warnings of severe reductions in the numbers of American tourists visiting Canada. Mr. William Duron, president of the Metropolitan Toronto Convention and Visitors Association, has stated: "If United States convention organizers have to live with an additional tax they will close the door on Canada".
In view of the overwhelming evidence that has been given in the last few days by the tourist industry of Canada, I would like to know from the minister why and how he can continue to say that the Canadian tourism industry will not be hurt in the years to come.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is important that we listen closely to all the tourist organizations in Canada when we bring in a replacement tax.
It is very important too that we realize this is not an additional tax. I wish members of the opposition would get this through their heads. It is a replacement of an old tax.
Oral Questions
The National Tourism Association of the United States is going to put together a suggestion and a mechanism on rebates that it would like to recommend to the government. All of this is progressing. It is progressing with a replacement tax, not an additional tax.

Mr. Speaker, if this is a replacement tax, what about a statement by the Deputy Minister of Finance, Mr. Dodge, who said, and I quote:

"Ordinary Canadians travelling on holidays will face higher prices, no question".

If it is true that Canadian tourists will have to pay more to travel in Canada, how does the minister explain his statement that this will be a replacement tax? The Minister of State (Finance) says it will cost more. Do you agree with that statement or could you explain why the situation is so complex?

That is very good news for the tourist industry and very good news for the hospitality industry.
In terms of the cost of running a tourist establishment, the hon. member constantly talks about the 7 per cent tax. What he forgets is the fact that the input tax credit will diminish that by 2, 3 or 4 per cent. So we will have a

slight increase. The Conference Board tells us after this tax is digested in two years we will have a net increase in tourism in three years, a greater increase than we would have had if we never had the GST in the first place.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
Yesterday, Bombardier announced that it would seek federal assistance to start up a high speed passenger train between Quebec City and Toronto. It says such a service would be profitable with 5.3 million passengers a year. It says that it can still charge less than airlines.
Bombardier has just confirmed what we have been saying all along. Passenger rail is the way of the future.
If the private sector has that kind of confidence in passenger rail, why doesn't the Government?
Hear, hear!

If the private sector can put $3.5 billion into a high speed train, then it is up to the private sector. Obviously, the government does not have that money to put into such an option.
I said yesterday that we will listen to what the private sector has to say about what it can do. We are interested by the proposal. However, once again, we do not have the money today to put $1.7 billion into any kind of train.

Given the comments the minister just made, that if the government at some point is prepared to consider financially supporting this particular proposal, will the minister give his assurance that instead of giving Bombardier-a private sector company-the funding, that he will invest that money in a public system so that all Canadians can share in the profit instead of just a few?

Mr. Speaker, I will not give any assurance to anybody. I will just wait for the royal commission to provide a few recommendations about passenger service in this country.
It is absolutely normal that we wait for the proposals to be made. That is why I think it would be wise for everyone to wait for the recommendations of the royal commission.

When will the government sit down with CREESOM?

course, Mr. Speaker, I will. I wrote to the chairman of the environmental assessment review panel to say that I never said that.

Mr. Speaker, with Canadian taxpayer assistance de Havilland developed the Dash-8 and was producing it in Canada for some 14 months before de Havilland was privatized to Boeing. As

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1984, when we took over government, one of the things we inherited was de Havilland, into which the taxpayers of Canada had poured $800 million and were looking at another $300 million at least before it could approach some sort of viability.
We had a choice of continuing that kind of contribution of taxpayers' money, closing it down for a cost of $300 million, or selling it to a private sector operator that could do a better job.
At the time, if the hon. member will take a look at the press releases, there was unconcluded liabilities that had to be met to the tune of $63 million. We have used DIPP to help fund the next generation of Dash aircraft. The plant has 1,000 more employees.
The taxes of those employees who are now working as a result of what we did will more than make up for the extra contribution. The hon. member should be applauding us, not criticizing us.

Mr. Speaker, I have petitions on three different subjects which have been sent to me by people from my riding.
The first petition calls upon the government to abandon its proposed goods and services tax. It proposes that the government reject the GST, cancel tax breaks for rich individuals and corporations, apply the present tax on goods manufactured in Canada equally to imported products, reduce the need for a sales tax by reducing the bank interest rate by 2 per cent, and increase employment in such useful work as protection of the environment, restoration of needed roads, sewers and bridges, air traffic control, VIA services, and industrial research and development.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a set of petitions from people in the riding who call upon the government to support VIA Rail, to abandon any plans for further cuts to VTA's budget, and to provide the necessary resources to allow VIA to operate as a modern effective transportation company rather than as a museum.

Mr. Speaker, the final petition is addressed to the government and is opposed to the government's proposed tax back of old age security and family allowance benefits.
The petitioners call upon the government to abandon this proposed measure which singles out old age security and family allowance benefits as a.tax source tied to the level of income.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to present a petition pursuant to Standing Order 36 and certified correct by the clerk of petitions. It is from a large number of constituents of my riding of Cochrane-Superior, more specifically from the towns of Longlac, Smooth Rock Falls, Val Rita, and Geraldton.
These residents are very concerned about a task force report on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas.
Routine Proceedings
This task force would see 37 communities in my riding no longer eligible for the tax benefit, thereby draining $2.5 million from the economy of Cochrane-Superior.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to reject the task force report in its totality.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the responsibility to table three petitions signed by residents of metropolitan Toronto surrounding Pearson International Airport.
As Your Honour knows, there has been much controversy in respect of the government's action on Pearson Airport, particularly with the continued expansion of the airport to the detriment of residents, their livelihoods and their investments in and around Pearson International Airport.
These petitioners who number in the hundreds, suggest and demand that the Government of Canada come down with a policy on three issues specifically.
First, that all aircraft must climb to 4,000 feet before banking over residential areas.
Second, that there be a strict enforcement of the night guidelines so that aircraft do not come in at all hours of the night and the morning as they do now and that they only permit emergency flights to do so.
Third, that they do not build an additional runway which will cause havoc in the surrounding areas, but rather that they suggest alternative airports be utilized in order to make passenger flights more comfortable and convenient for Canadians and that there must be a sensitivity to those surrounding communities.

Mr. Speaker, I have a petition, signed by several hundred residents of my constituency from the communities of Courtenay, Comox, Cumberland, Port Alberni, Coombs, Errington, Parksville, Qualicum Beach and Royston, among others.
They request the government to reject the current proposal for a goods and services tax, to reform the taxation system so that there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations, and to cease with a proposal which will shift the tax burden on to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reform.

February 14, 1990
Routine Proceedings
I also have a petition which was put together by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, through one of its associate members, Clarence's Brake and Repair, in my riding. There are several hundreds of names attached to this petition, but unfortunately it is not in a form that could be certified.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition from my riding which was circulated by the seniors organization One Voice. It calls on the government to scrap its proposal to claw back pensions and family allowances and begin to treat seniors and family members fairly in the tax system.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my pleasure to rise in the House to present a number of petitions from British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario.
The petitioners voice their opposition to the goods and services tax proposed by this government. They petition the government to ensure that, if and when there is a broad public consensus on a sales tax measure to replace the manufacturers' sales tax, this reform not be an opportunity for the government to impose a massive tax grab.

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition according to the Standing Orders from a number of residents of the province of Ontario who oppose the government's proposal for a goods and services tax. They ask for a tax system that will give an effective minimum tax on wealthy individuals and corporations and ensure that there is no taxation on goods and services such as haircuts, fast food, piano lessons and other non-luxury items.
The petitioners wish Parliament to cause the government to cease the proposal that will tax diapers and coffins, taxing Canadians from the cradle to the grave.

Mr. Speaker, I also have a petition from a number of residents of Toronto who are concerned with the government's proposed
increase of low-level flights in Labrador over the land of the Innu.
The petitioners ask that this Parliament join with the Assembly of First Nations and the Innu people in demanding that the Canadian government end NATO-NORAD low-level flight training, oppose the establishment of NATO operations in Canada such as at Goose Bay, redirect Canada's NATO-NORAD funding toward enabling Canada's aboriginal peoples to regain control of their lands and their livelihood, and promote sustainable development for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I also have petitions from a number of residents of Ontario in Stratford, Hamilton, Chatham, Sudbury, Timmins, Orillia, Brampton, Windsor, Belleville, Toronto, Downsview, Cayuga, Westhill, Barrie, Ottawa, Welland and Kitchener.
They are concerned with the government's proposal to reduce VIA Rail service. They ask this Parliament to reject all reductions, to modernize existing equipment so that VIA Rail can provide a world-class service and to build a high speed passenger train between Montreal and Windsor.

Mr. Speaker, I have a number of petitions from people of my constituency representing various groups: farm and ranch groups, hotel and motel operators, restaurants, fishing and hunting resorts, a variety of small businesses, arts groups, student groups, environment groups, bowling associations, A&W and McDonald's patrons.
They point out the unfairness of the goods and services tax. They feel that it is an unfair tax and simply make the point that the government should go back to the drawing board, try again with real fair tax reform and stop proceeding with this 7 per cent goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I also have two petitions with quite a number of signatures. Some of them are from people in southern Ontario and others are from citizens of British Columbia.
I think they epitomize the fact that people right across this country are asking the government to reject the proposed goods and services tax, to reform the tax system so there is an effective minimum tax on wealthy

individuals and corporations, and to cease with a proposal that will shift the burden to ordinary Canadians through a regressive consumption tax instead of through real tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, I too have the privilege of rising under Standing Order 36. Many residents within my riding of Essex-Kent also suggest that the goods and services tax is inappropriate and one that is going to cause them difficulty with thenway of living.
They humbly ask the government to withdraw its proposed goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I rise, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present petitions on behalf of my constituents from the riding of Mississauga East who are outraged at this government's heavy-handed manner in imposing additional runways at Pearson International.
My constituents are concerned that this action will have negative impact on their quality of life. They humbly pray and call upon Parliament to start heeding their concerns.

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, I would like to present a petition signed by a number of British Columbians, including a number of residents of my own riding of Surrey North.
It states that the government has not addressed the unfair tax system currently in place which permits wealthy individuals and corporations to pay little or no federal tax, while forcing low and middle income taxpayers to bear more of the national tax. They call upon this government to institute genuine tax reform.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today, under the provisions of Standing Order 36, to present a petition concerning the government's proposed goods and services tax.
Routine Proceedings
The petition is signed by concerned Canadians who feel that this tax will cause serious and unfair hardship to lower and middle income Canadians.
The petitioners call upon Parliament to reject the goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that I have to rise again to bring this matter to the attention of the Chair.
Question No. 162, standing in my name, has been on the Order Paper, not for 45 days but since October 30, 1989, which is against the rules of this House. Your Honour will note that the question is properly identified as being one of those it is compulsory for the government to reply to within 45 days.
I want further to bring to your attention, Mr. Speaker, that there is another question in exactly the same situation, that being Question No. 197 in my name, which was placed on the Order Paper on December 6, 1989.
In fact I have four questions on the Order Paper in my name, all requiring answers. Because the government is failing to respond to these questions I cannot place new questions on the Order Paper. In other words, I am prevented from doing my work as a member of Parliament because of the inaction of the government.
I alert the Chair to this issue. I have brought it to the attention of the Chair before. This is a new Standing Order. It has only been with us for a few years now. The government just cannot say that it answers appropriately a certain percentage of the time. This rule is quite clear. It must do so 100 per cent of the time.
I asked the parliamentary secretary to bring this matter to the attention of the officials in question, to make sure that they get off their duffs, or however the Minister for International Trade refers to it, and attend to these replies in the manner they are required to according to the rules of this place.

February 14, 1990

Mr. Speaker, we are looking forward to beginning debate on Bill C-52 later today and we will see
Business of the House
how progress is made for tomorrow. There have been discussions and like my hon. friend the House Leader for the Official Opposition, we too will attempt to expedite this legislation which we support in terms of needed legislation. The House resumed from Tuesday, January 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre) that Bill C-52, an act to amend the Income Tkx Act and related acts, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to join with my colleagues in the New Democratic Party to oppose second reading of Bill C-52.
Bill C-52 is fundamentally a bill to make changes in the RRSP legislation and other similar tax assistance schemes that have prevailed in this country for almost 20 years. The bill increases the current limits under which Canadian taxpayers can get tax assistance or reduce their taxes by virtue of investments in RRSPs and provides that the increased limits will be indexed over a period of time.
The current limits for RRSPs are about $7,500 or 20 per cent of income. The proposed limit would increase over a period of time. Starting in 1991 the limit would go to $11,500; in 1992 to $12,500; in 1993 to $13,500; in 1994 to $14,500; and by 1995 the limit would reach $15,500. After that period these limits would be indexed to increases in wages and salaries. The bill also provides for what is called a "carry-over" provision so that in a given year those who cannot contribute or choose not to contribute to an RRSP can pick up that difference for a period of time.
This bill affects a transfer of tax money in the order of $5 billion to $6 billion yearly, when it comes into full force, from lower and middle-income taxpayers to the wealthy and better off income tax payers in this country. It undermines the possibilities of improving the Canada Pension Plan, the Quebec Pension Plan and the Old Age Assistance Program.
It undermines the possibility of developing a proper public pension plan system in this country to provide fairness and equity to the people of Canada. It encourages the development of privatization of pensions and contributes to a tendency which appears to be the

underlying philosophy of this government; to make the rich richer and the middle and low-income groups poorer.
Let us take a step back in the history of the development of public pension policy in this country. We in this party are proud of the role played by our predecessors in this House, starting with J. S. Woodsworth in 1926 who used his position in Parliament to force out of a reluctant Liberal government the first old age pensions in Canada.
Canadians will be familiar with the long battle led by the former hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, Mr. Stanley Knowles, to make old age pensions universal and to eliminate the means test. That battle was won.
Then there was the battle to develop a proper Canada Pension Plan into which employers and employees would contribute and which would provide a further basis for a secure future for seniors in this country. This was achieved in 1964.
Then, in the early seventies, came the first RRSP program. Originally the RRSP program was designed to provide opportunities for those who were not covered by employer sponsored programs, the normal pension programs that employees could participate in to provide those people with an opportunity to build their own pension plans and their own economic security in addition to the Old Age Security system.
It was also expected that those who had employer sponsored programs could use the RRSP program to supplement further their retirement income because at the beginning, and as presently prevails, the Canada Pension Plan together with Old Age Security still does not meet the full retirement needs of Canadians. It only brings the retirement income up into the order of 40 per cent to 50 per cent of pre-retirement income. All those who have studied this field say that a good system would provide closer to 75 per cent of pre-retirement income as the basic level of retirement income that would provide for a secure future for senior citizens.
The RRSPs had these two objectives: to provide an opportunity for those who are not covered by employer sponsored plans, and to provide for a supplement to the Canada Pension Plan or Quebec Pension Plan in the
Government Orders
event they were insufficient which, of course, has happened and was predictable.
Those at the lower and middle income levels whose incomes are barely sufficient and in some cases insufficient to meet their daily, weekly and monthly income needs do not have any money left over to respond to the myriad of ads that we now see on television and in the media encouraging Canadians to invest in RRSPs. It is only those with extra income, the upper half of the income group, who can begin to think of taking advantage of the RRSP provisions in the Income Tax Act. As a result the experience has been that the benefits of RRSP programs go in the largest measure to the top 5 per cent of the income groups in Canada.
This bill will make that inequity even worse. Under the provisions of this bill the single mother on welfare can, if she chooses, contribute $11,500 of her income every year to an RRSP. Her income does not even meet $11,500 a year. Therefore, it will come as no surprise that what we have here is a bonanza for the financial institutions in this country and a bonanza for those in the upper income group who can afford to take advantage of this tax assistance scheme.
The government is introducing legislation which is a benefit for the rich and is simply not available to the poor and middle income groups in this country. It is going to cost the Canadian taxpayers $5 billion to $6 billion a year to implement this scheme.
Next week we are going to hear from the Minister of Finance-we have already seen the balloons go up-that this budget is going to be a Draconian, cut-back budget. It is going to cut again at public services to this country. Yet merely a week before the budget the government is persisting with a bill which is a $5 billion to $6 billion give-away to the upper income group in this country. This bill must be defeated.
It is important for this House to understand as well that the way this bill is structured, the government is persisting in using the device of tax deductions rather than tax credits. The $11,500 under the RRSP that is included here becomes a deduction from income. The government is not using a tax credit system. Most Canadians will now understand the significance of that difference. A tax credit system means that regardless of income the benefit of the particular provision is equal-

ized. A tax deduction system benefits, again, those at the higher income levels.
Once again, the provisions of the bill in keeping with the reactionary philosophy of this government assists those in the highest income groups.
Let me refer the House to an editorial from The Toronto Star which commented when this bill was first floated on October 16, 1986, that: "The distribution of income in Canada is highly unequal. In 1981, the 20 per cent of Canadian families with the highest incomes ended up with 41.8 per cent of the total income pie. By contrast, 20 per cent of the families with the lowest incomes get less than 5 per cent."
The editorial goes on to state: "Under Wilson's new proposals, Ottawa would provide tax assistance to all employed Canadians to create a nest-egg that would allow them to maintain their incomes in retirement, up to a pension limit of $60,000 a year. To do so, he would provide the greatest assistance to those at the upper end of the income scale. Someone earning $20,000 a year, would get an annual tax break worth about $1,200, compared to a break of about $7,500 for those earning more than $86,000 a year."
I may add that the break for the person earning $20,000 a year is only available, of course, if that person has the spare cash at the end of the year to contribute toward an RRSP or one of the other plans covered in this bill.
In a fair and proper pension system, instead of investing the $5 and $6 billion that this government is prepared to give away to the top income groups in this country, this money would be used to strengthen the Old Age Security system and the Canada Pension Plan. In 1983, there was a parliamentary task force on pension reform. It became very clear from that task force that the real reform in this country needed to be the strengthening of the Canada Pension Plan. Virtually every member of the paid workforce, with earnings from employment or self-employment, is covered by the CPP, in contrast to those who can afford the benefits under RRSP provisions.
Many witnesses before the task force, including those representing workers and women, recommended a doubling of Canada and Quebec Pension Plan benefits to 50 per cent of pre-retirement earnings, up to the annual amount allowed. This increase, of course, has to be phased in over a period of time. But if we have those
kind of changes, we would be spending public money in accordance with proper principles of public policy. A pension program in this country should produce a fair and equitable distribution of income at retirement. It should produce a satisfactory level of income and should be contributed to in a fair and just manner.
In this case the lower and middle income taxpayers who pay the largest portion of taxes in this country are contributing to the ultimate income advantage and short-term tax benefit of the highest income groups in the country.
The parliamentary task force noted that only half of men and fewer than one third of women who are in the paid workforce are covered by the Canada Pension Plan. That should be changed. They note that when people change jobs it is difficult to get the additional coverage because of long waiting periods.
Benefits in the private pension system are barely covered by inflation. The real reform in this country should come in the area of the Canada Pension Plan. That is the policy of this party and that is the policy that we urge upon the House.
My closing remarks will deal first with one other specific problem with this legislation, and that is its complexity. In May 1988 the joint committee on taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants described these amendments as "perhaps the most complicated tax rules ever devised".
These provisions will employ chartered accountants, any who are left over after the GST, in years and hours of complex analysis because of the complexity of the new rules. In fact most individual taxpayers will not be able to calculate the allowable RRSP contributions. At the beginning of each tax year the federal government will provide to each taxpayer a statement of available RRSP contribution room. To determine this amount, pension plan administrators will be required to submit a detailed report of each plan member's earnings for the year and the amount of the plan member's pension adjustment.
Revenue Canada will use this information based on previous contributions to calculate the following year's RRSP contribution availability. This situation makes it virtually impossible for individuals to engage in any kind of long-term financial planning. In addition, the rules will make it extremely difficult for small pension plan

administrators to function without hiring additional staff solely responsible for pension adjustment reporting.
The Canadian Council on Social Development has stated in respect of a predecessor to this bill:
We are starting to replace a progressive and visible benefits system with hidden subsidies that are in fact regressive. For example, we may eliminate the Old Age Security benefits among higher-income people -
That is the clawback:
-but for the generation who will be seniors when this measure has its full impact, we are more than replacing them by increasing the limits on RRSP deductions and by putting in place a capital gains exemption. These kinds of measures provide high levels of subsidy, higher than the cut in the Old Age Security to high-income people.
Bill C-52 allows high income earners whose Old Age Security will be clawed back to more than compensate for the lost income by making increased contributions to RRSP. Meanwhile, because of the lack of inflation indexing in the clawback, future pensioners will see their Old Age Security clawed back at lower and lower income levels.
These policies, when fit together, spell the true intention of this government. It is to serve the better off in this society. This bill does not meet the test of what it will do for the least of these in our society. This will provide no assistance for the least of these in our society and therefore this bill is wrong in principle, wrong in practice, and must be opposed.
I would like to move an amendment:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "that" and substituting therefor:

The position of the elderly in Canada has improved, particularly when it comes to income and financial security. It has improved mainly through the introduction of old age security and the Canada Pension Plan. Those are the two vehicles that Canada has used to provide universal and equitable pensions.
The only problem with the Canada Pension Plan and old age security is that initially it was intended to be extended. In the last number of years the scope of the Canada Pension Plan and the contributing factor has been diminished and the government has more and more looked on private pension plans, whether they are run by unions, by corporations and upon the RRSP program to allow the elderly to look after themselves in their old age. That is fine for people in the unionized workforce where they have good private pension plans. It has not worked for those who are in non-union or service jobs where there is no company or government-sponsored pension plans.
The RRSP has been nothing but a tax grab for the wealthy. It has nothing to do with providing universal high-calibre pensions for all Canadians.
If we look at the whole question of who contributes to RRSPs, one of the first things we will find is that not all Canadians are involved. Those on very limited incomes do not contribute. In fact, those with total incomes of less than $5,000, only .9 per cent contribute; those with incomes of $5,000 to $10,000, 3.7 per cent contribute. When we get up to those earning $25,000 nearly 33 per cent of taxpayers contribute to RRSPs. Those with incomes up to $50,000, 57 per cent contribute to RRSPs. So there is a disproportionate rate of participation in RRSP programs based on the level of income.
It is very simple. There is nothing mystical about it. The family man earning $25,000 does not have additional money that he can put in the bank for his old age regardless of whether there is a tax break or incentive to do that. The person earning over $50,000 has disposable income and he puts it aside for his old age. But he does not do it on an equal basis as the person earning $25,000. He does it with tax incentives that are much greater.
One of the real anomalies in the question of RRSPs is that if a person in the lower tax bracket of $20,000 makes a contribution of $1,000, he gets $264 back in a tax break. But if a person on a low income can afford to contribute, he or she will get $264 back for every $1,000 contributed. If a person in the highest tax bracket contributes $1,000, he or she gets $450 back. What kind of system gives the wealthy twice as much cash back as the poor?
That is the whole structure of the RRSP program. It is really an incentive for the wealthy to put aside money for their old age so they can have their retirement in comfort in Hawaii, Florida or the Bahamas. It is not designed to ensure that women who have worked all their lives at jobs paying $15,000 a year can afford to have adequate housing, food, clothing and transportation when they reach an elderly age.
