I also want to refer to the fact that very few older women in Canada are eligible for the Canada Pension Plan because many of them have been homemakers or they have come into the labour market very late. They have not been able to build up sufficient points for adequate income from that source.
I cannot recall myself, but I wonder if he would clarify that the GIS is not indexed. I think that is correct. Certainly, the Conservatives tried to deindex the old age pension itself and seniors said they would not have that.
The other thing perhaps he might comment on is the fact that, and this is an item he is quite an expert in, we hear very worrisome rumours that the federal transfer payments for the Canada Assistance Plan are likely to be restricted. This will have a tremendous impact on social services of all kinds and, particularly, income support

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
programs for older people. I wonder if he would comment on those items.

Mr. Speaker, the hon member for Vancouver East has raised a number of very critical questions in areas that I could spend another half-hour discussing.
I want to comment on the last one particularly because it is going to be one of the major issues that this House has to deal with in the next period of time. It is the rumours that the Canada Assistance Plan, which has been an open-ended, cost-sharing program with the provinces, is somehow going to be limited.
The people who are going to be hurt are those on various types of social assistance programs or those who are on supplementary programs for the elderly. The provincial governments can and do supplement through the Canada Assistance Plan types of income support and care programs for the elderly. I keep coming back to the fact that one of the things that we still have not fundamentally addressed in this bill is the discrepancy in income security between men and women in this country, particularly over the age of 65.
I would just like to point out a couple of figures. In 1971, the average income from all sources for men was $12,500. For women it was $6,183. By 1986, for men it had increased to $16,700, which is getting up to $1,500 a month. For women it was still just over $10,000, which is $800 a month. You cannot live in metropolitan areas and pay rent, buy food, have transportation and medical care on that level of income.

Mr. Speaker, in the member's comments he referred to benefiting the rich in our society and hurting the lower income people. I wonder if he would comment on the fact that there is a seven-year carry forward in this particular act resulting in a young family, or someone going into the labour force, having this seven-year carry forward of an unused contribution. As well, the limits will be frozen until 1995. If you look at 1995, it is interesting to note that the $15,500 limit in that year will be the same fraction of the average industrial wage as the limit of $4,900 in 1976 when the limit was $5,500.

Mr. Speaker, the member raises a point of this carry-over. That is all very nice. The trouble is that if you cannot afford to do it this year, you cannot afford to do it next year or the year after, the likelihood that in seven years from now when you are still supporting your family and still on an income of $27,000 that you could then afford to do it not only for that year but for the past ten, seven or five years is just nonsense.
All it is going to do is make sure that the wealthy, who maybe for some reason this year have a little problem with cash flow because they bought another investment or they put money into an apartment block, can pick up on it next year.
I do not see it as any incentive for the poor, or even the people on middle incomes, I see it just as another give-a-way for the wealthy to make sure that their cash flow is not hurt when they invest in RRSPs.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: The time for questions and comments has expired. On debate, the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak on the amendment. I think it is a valid amendment in that it points out with some clarity the New Democratic Party position on this particular bill. I would like for the record to read again, for emphasis, the two points that are made:
(1)	the full benefit of the increased registered retirement savings
plan limit will accrue only to the less than 1 per cent of Canadian
taxpayers who earn more than $86,000 annually.
I will comment on that in a minute.
The second point:
(2)	it fails-assist middle and lower income Canadians to provide
for a stable income in their retirement years.
Now, I think the first point is the crux of the whole problem with this government's thrust toward tax reform, toward many of the programs that we have seen instituted over the last five years. Whether it be the Unemployment Insurance Act changes, free trade, or the clawback, it emphasizes to all Canadians what is happening.
The program that we see before us, as was emphasized to me as I travelled across Canada with the finance committee, emphasizes the polarity between the rich and the poor. This is of major concern to me and the New Democratic Party and to many Canadians to whom I and
February 14, 1990

others have spoken with regard to the direction in which this government appears to be going.
The government should be ensuring for future generations some balance in the incomes of Canadians, an equality of life for Canadians, whether in their own homes, their communities, their provinces or their regions. Canadians should be able to hold their heads high with the knowledge that there is economic and environmental equality. Instead, we are seeing this polarity.
The rich appear to be getting the benefit. As my grandfather used to say, "Them what has gets". I think that is exactly what is happening here. The rich are getting richer, the poor are getting poorer. If we continue with this particular agenda, fewer and fewer middle-income people will to be able to live with their heads high. By this type of legislation we are forcing those who are a little less fortunate into becoming poverty stricken and increasing the distance between the middle income-earners and the rich, those who have.
The major thrust, I would suggest, to the New Democratic Party's position is not to increase or expand upon this polarity, but to move toward the equality that we in Canada have come to expect of each other and of our governments. The thrust in any legislation, whether it be social or pension legislation, should be a thrust of equality, a thrust of fairness, something that people can look to and say: "That will help all Canadians, not just a limited few".
The suggestion of the New Democratic Party is that we should not be looking at the upper end of the scale. We should be looking at the over-all picture of universal pensions for women, for men, for rich and for poor alike, something portable, something that we can hold on and look forward to so as to ensure that we can live comfortably in our golden years. We do not have to live with all the baubles, bangles, gold and silver and all that glitters. It is a matter of comfort and having what is necessary or essential to be able to carry on and live in dignity in those retiring years.
I would suggest the way to do that is through our Canada Pension Plan system, ensuring that that plan is portable and adequate and treats men and women alike
Government Orders
with equality. We have seen for too long all the problems which women have run into with husbands' pensions.
As I said earlier, women make 65 per cent of what males make on average. I would suggest that this in itself shows the inequality within our system. We must strive for greater things than simply looking to a small section with blinders on. It is a broader perspective. It is something that we should be working toward together too ensure the equality and fairness that I spoke of earlier.
At present, under the proposed legislation, at the end of 1995 those who make $86,111 will be able to put in the maximum $15,500. This scales up over a five-year period. Again, it emphasizes that those who will be able to use the upper limit are those with the higher incomes, those who probably already have other investments, who have put money away in other things, who are looking after themselves and have the maximum Canada Pension Plan.
I am not saying that they should not put money away for their future in Registered Retirement Savings Plans and the New Democratic Party is not saying that we are against Registered Retirement Savings Plans. We have never said that. We are saying that we are looking in the wrong direction. We should be looking at the area of universality of our pension plans.
There should be a cap placed on those pension plans. I do not think the dropping from 20 per cent to 18 per cent of earnings assists the middle and low-income earners. That, it seems to me, tends to hurt the low and middle-income earners and assists those in the upper-income area.
I would suggest that the seven-year carry-forward contained in this legislation again, as has been emphasized by my friend from Surrey North, is more an advantage for those people with higher incomes and the ability to invest. Yes, from the perspective of a small business person who one year, if the economy picks up, may have a little bit of extra money, it has a certain flavour of advantage.
But if we look at who uses the Registered Retirement Savings Plan area, I think it becomes fairly clear that those who will use the seven-year carry-forward provision are in fact those who want to use their money for some specific tax advantage investment one year and then pick it up a year or two later when they reap the

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
benefits of that investment. But the low-income earner, unless he wins a lottery, is not going to have the money that is required to take advantage of that seven-year carry-forward.
So while I am saying that the carry-forward will assist some of the middle-income earners in some way, it is going to be a small percentage of those earners. The rich, again, will be the ones taking advantage of it.
I have referred to the number of tax filers who contribute to RRSPs in trying to emphasize my point of the carry-forward. In 1987, the last year for which I have figures, 57.8 per cent of those with incomes of $50,000 and over made an average contribution was $4,700. If we look at the other end of the scale, 3.7 per cent of those who earn from $5,000 to $10,000 contributed to RRSPs. Let us take a look at the middle incomes, $30,000 to $40,000. The proportion of tax filers who contributed to RRSPs in that tax bracket was 40.4 per cent, contributing an average contribution of $2,480. The maximum in 1987, of course, had just gone up to $7,500, so that is well below the average. It is apparent that these people are not going to be able to afford to use the seven-year carry-forward.
There are other problems in this bill. This is a complex bill and I do not pretend to totally understand everything about it. I do not pretend to know all there is to know about Registered Retirement Savings Plans as I am sure the Minister of Finance, who is working in this area constantly, would not claim to know everything about it.
The minister points out that the government is trying to cover loopholes. That could well be, but I am sure the minister knows as well as most lawyers, that as soon as you change any legislation there are minds out there that are quick and sly like the fox, able to ferret out and find loopholes. Being a lawyer I can confirm that every time new legislation comes up it leads to a wide range of new technical arguments. The tax area, which is one of the most complex areas of law in Canada, I would suggest, certainly leads to that.
In May of 1988, the joint committee on taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants called the amendments perhaps the most complicated tax rules ever devised. In order to calculate tax-free Registered Retirement Savings Plan
contribution limits for those who are members of retirement savings plans, the legislation establishes a formula. You take the Registered Retirement Savings Plan limit, which is 18 per cent or the dollar maximum, and subtract from it the pension adjustment. In the case of the money purchase plans, the pension adjustment is simply the annual total of the employer-employee contributions. For defined benefit plan members, which are 90 per cent of those covered by private plans, the pension adjustment equals the annual benefit earned multiplied by a factor of nine minus 600. Clear to you, Mr. Speaker? And that is the simple part of it.
I would suggest that because of the complexity of the new rules, most individual taxpayers will no longer be able to calculate their allowable RRSP contribution room. At the beginning of each tax year the federal government will provide to each taxpayer a statement of available RRSP contribution room. To determine this amount, pension plan administrators will be required to submit a detailed report of each plan member's earnings for the year and the amount of the plan member's pension adjustment. Revenue Canada will use this information, based on the previous year's RRSP contributions, to calculate the following year's RRSP contribution.
This situation makes it virtually impossible for individuals to engage in any kind of long-term financial planning. In addition, the rules will make it extremely difficult for small pension plan administrators to function without hiring additional staff solely responsible for pension adjustment reporting.
We are asking the government to take the blinders off, to quit looking through this limited vision tunnel and to look at the broader expanse of where we are going in this society in this country. Let us get some real reform. Let us get proper pension reform so that, as I said earlier, people can feel there is equality and fairness in Canada for all Canadians, regardless of how they have made out income-wise in their younger years, so that they can live adequately in their golden years, with respect and dignity. Let this government hear the people of Canada. Let this government recognize that the future is not in this narrow vein. The future for Canadians, as has been set out by our forefathers, is one of assistance and equality for all.
February 14, 1990

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the NDP often speak as if there is a huge group of people in this country who make vast amounts of money and are very rich. I would refer him, as a new member, to the income tax statistics. They are exactly the same, percentage-wise, over the years. If a Canadian makes $30,000 total income, not net, that person, in terms of taxpayers, is already just over the 85 percentile. So less than 15 per cent of Canadians make over $30,000 gross income.
If a person's income is $50,000, that person is at 98.15. So less than 1.5 per cent of taxpayers make more than $50,000. That tells you there is not some huge number of vastly rich people out there. We are they. We make $60,000, and we are 99 per cent. Nobody makes more than us. So this whole pension plan is to let people like us take a deduction during our working years and build up a pension. If that does not work we will have to be content with the Canada Pension, for what that is worth, and the Old Age Security and the GIS.
My specific question is this: Is it NDP policy to be opposed to the RRSP? That is a major policy change. I admire them, but I want to be able to go up to the doorsteps and say: "Is it your policy, or is it not"?

Mr. Speaker, even though my friend was there, I think what he has emphasized to the people of Canada, what we have been telling them in the House of Commons and what the people of Canada have been telling them ever since I was elected here in 1988 is: "You are listening, but you do not hear". If the hon. member had not only listened but heard, he would have heard me say that it is not the New Democratic Party policy to do away with Registered Retirement Savings Plans.
It is obvious that the hon. member has done exactly what the Minister of Finance has been doing, what the Minister of Employment and Immigration has been doing and what the Prime Minister and his party have done in the free trade debate. They have listened and they have listened well, but just like the dopes that I believe they must be, they have not heard. I would suggest to those members that they should take out the earplugs, open their ears, quit sitting there in their fog and listen to the people of Canada and hear what they are saying.
Government Orders
I would like to turn for a minute to something this hon. member has told us. I think he has made the point very well, that is, this government is controlled by 1.5 per cent of the people of Canada, those higher income earners. It is the other 98.5 per cent to whom this government should start listening. They have been ignored for too long. People can only be pushed so long before they revolt. This government more and more is heading for that revolt.
That is the case not only in taxation but in other areas such as racial discrimination. This polarity is pushing people into economic hardship. As the hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair said yesterday in his wonderful speech, this government's policies are causing problems across Canada and it is time that it started hearing the people.

Mr. Speaker, on rising to speak in opposition to Bill C-52, which would raise the limits for RRSP purchases to $15,500 over a five-year period, I could not help but think that politics is about making choices.
We are constantly lectured by people on the other side that we on this side of the House do not give a damn about debt, do not give a damn about deficits. That is not true. If anything points out the reality, if there is anything in this House which does not take deficits and debt seriously, it is this bill proposed by that bunch over there.
What is the impact of this legislation in terms of cost? Currently tax assistance for retirement savings costs the federal treasury an estimated $5 billion to $6 billion each year in foregone tax revenues. This new legislation will cost an additional $300 million to $350 million in 1991-1992 alone. That does not seem like a lot of money to some people in accordance with the size of the entire federal budget. However, to give an example, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety is being junked by this government to save $10 million a year. That serves millions of working Canadians and their employers and is one thing that this government is shoving into the garbage can, along with the lives of thousands of Canadian workers, all for a measly $10 million, while here it gives $300 million to $350 million a year to people in our income category who do not really need the extra help.

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
Politics is about making choices. The title underneath this bill should be a paraphrase of the old quotation that the law in all its majestic equality provides that rich and poor alike may put $15,000 a year into RRSPs in order to avoid paying taxes. That would be just as hypocritical as the original saying that rich and poor alike are forbidden to sleep under bridges. It is exactly the same message.
This government is scrapping the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety to save $10 million a year. It has, to save some $500 million to $600 million a year, just about double what it is throwing away by this mechanism, ditched a rail system from one end of the country to the other. This has ended up effectively isolating many small resource communities in areas that do not have other effective means of transportation. Despite what the government says about some of those communities, they do not.
The government would not listen. It said that we have got to save the money. Yet here it is giving away half that amount of money because people in our income categories need its help so much. Like hell we do. We don't need that kind of help.
At the same time the government has sabotaged the UIC system to increase premiums for employers, whether or not they are making a profit, and employees alike, supposedly to save money, thereby creating another total aberration and turning upside down any idea of a progressive tax system. Withdrawing any support of the UIC system from general revenue has removed any incumbency upon the government to keep employment levels high and removed the incentive to keep employment levels high, because the government wants to save money. And then it gives away $300 million or $350 million a year to people like us who do not really need the additional help.
There is one last thing I want to mention because it really draws some of the priorities of this government into question. The government has recently imposed increases in municipal radio licence fees from one end of the country to the other.
In my community alone volunteers in fire departments and individuals who sacrifice a lot of their time, money and effort in order to provide emergency services to their
neighbours find that their municipal, regional or county governments are being slapped with increased radio licence fees to provide for those basic emergency services that are health providing and life saving.
For a small community like my own in Nelson, British Columbia, that increase is 1,200 per cent this year. For the city of Trail, it is a 970 per cent increase in those radio licence fees. For the regional district of Kootenay boundary, it is a 1,789 per cent increase.
It is not enough for people on the government side to say: "Oh yes, but we have to encourage people to save a little more". Politics is about making choices. The government is constantly preaching that. This is one of the choices it has made.
The government has said that those who provide basic emergency services in local communities can go out and hang themselves. They do not count. They can pay extra. It is telling the workers and small employers of Canada who need information on health and safety that their problems are not important, that they ought to pay for their own health services and for their own health information.
The government is telling the unemployed and small employers across the country that they can afford to pay more in UIC premiums, and that people in our income category can have extra incentives to help ourselves at the expense of the general public.
I for one cannot buy that that is an intelligent political choice, a rational political choice or a moral political choice. It is immoral, it is impractical and it is wrong. Members opposite are making the wrong choices. We believe that there are better choices in maintaining and building an improved public pension system in Canada.
We are not talking about scrapping RRSPs. They are now an integrated part of the Canadian pension system, and it is appropriate, but the extent to which the government is going to increase their availability is damaging. Many people within the pension and insurance industry are telling them and have told them that they are damaging the very public and private pension system in this country upon which thousands and millions of ordinary Canadians depend.
Their choice is wrong. It is wrong headed. It is immoral. That is why we oppose this bill. I would ask
February 14, 1990

members opposite to remember why they are here, who they ought to be representing, and vote accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the member. In 1983 Doug Frith was the chairman of a task force that looked very extensively at pension review. Would the hon. member let us know what aspects of this bill are in accord with the recommendations of the Frith commission and which ones are not?

Mr. Speaker, I was here in 1983. A number of years has gone by since, including four years off for good behaviour during which time I had other priorities.
I am afraid I cannot recall the provisions of Mr. Frith's proposals in order to be able to answer the question clearly as to whether or not this falls within that ambit.

I suffered the same fate for four years.
It dealt with the portability of pensions. It dealt with the indexing of pensions. It dealt with tax credits for pensions, particularly for the low income pensioner. Were any of these provisions included in this bill?
Mr. Speaker, from my perusal of this bill the answer would be no.

Mr. Speaker, I find it odd that we should be debating this bill. That is to say I find it odd that this measure should have been a priority of the government, when I remember the Conservatives in opposition making political careers, some of them, out of promising various groups of pensioners in Canada that once they came to power they would address the needs that had gone unmet under a Liberal administration.
The group of pensioners that I am thinking of in particular, probably because I have so many of them in my riding-indeed, I probably have more of them than any other member of Parliament, I would be willing to bet-is CN pensioners. Perhaps some of them now live in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt. I know some of them like to migrate out there in order to escape Winnipeg weather.
The fact remains that many promises were made to the CN pensioners by the Conservatives leading up to the election of 1984. The only thing that happened was that in the early years of the last Parliament in 1985 there was a special subcommittee which concerned itself with CN pensions. It made a number of recommendations. The
Government Orders
report as a whole was not exactly what the various CN pensioners associations and advocates like Earl White and others wanted. Nevertheless had the recommendations been approved it would have been an improvement on the situation.
It is now six years since 1984 and not a blessed thing has been done about CN pensions. We do not even hear anything about it any more. It is like it is a dead issue, something that belongs to prehistoric political time. It is not because CN pensioners are all gone. They are still out there watching their pension incomes, their retirement incomes, progressively decline because their pensions are not indexed.
This problem is understandably more severe for those who retired a long time ago and whose retirement incomes have been progressively eroded by inflation and the rising cost of living. Yet nothing is done for these folks, unless one is able to imagine that the majority of people on CN pensions are in the category of people who would be able to take advantage of the increase provided in this bill vis-a-vis money that may be used for RRSP purposes.
I can tell you, Mr. Speaker, there are very few CN pensioners in my riding-in fact it would be difficult to find any-who would say: "Oh, boy, I can put up to $15,000 a year now in RRSPs, so I don't have to worry that there is no improvement in the CN pension plan and that the Conservatives haven't lived up to their promises to CN pensioners. I can now take advantage of the provisions in this particular bill".
You know as well as I do, Mr. Speaker, that those kinds of CN pensioners do not exist. They are only a representative sample of many other working people who have worked for other companies, private or public, and who have pension plans that need to be improved and also need to incorporate indexing which has not happened to date.
The government has not moved on that broad front of pension reform on which, I must say, in the early eighties there seemed to be some momentum toward doing. We had the report of the task force mentioned by a member just a few minutes ago. Doug Frith, the former member for Sudbury, was the chairman of that task force. We had a number of other commissions and task forces. In fact, we were buried in these kinds of reports and analyses. A

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
great deal of good work was done at that time by one of our own colleagues, the hon. member for Beaches.
It seemed that we were at the point where we were going to have some genuine pension reform and that some of the problems that had been accumulating and worsening in the seventies and early eighties were going to be addressed. Then what happened? It is clear what happened. The Tories were elected in 1984. They made Liberal stagnation with respect to pension income look like movement.
The whole question of pension reform simply dropped into the political Bermuda Triangle called the Tory right wing agenda. Never again did we hear anything about comprehensive pension reform. Never again after the subcommittee report on CN pensions did we hear anything about reforming the CN pension plan or any other pension plan of that sort.
Instead, we had the Minister of Finance saying things like: "The problem with Canada is that we do not have enough rich people". Do you remember when he said that, Mr. Speaker? It is not that we have too many poor people. It is not that we have a massive problem with child poverty. It is not that we have the feminization of poverty in elder years with respect to elderly women. It is not that any of the problems that have been pointed out by so many people with respect to the problems of ordinary Canadians are our greatest problems.
No, as far as the Minister of Finance is concerned, the problem with Canada is that we do not have enough rich people. I will never forget what I think was the most revealing moment, the moment that in a way will never leave me.
I saw clearly into the consciousness of the collective Conservative mind, and it was a dark thing to behold. It was the night of the first budget of this particular government when the Minister of Finance announced the $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption. For the first time that evening all members of the government rose as one and gave the Minister of Finance a standing ovation because he had finally done the thing that would be so beneficial to the kinds of people who really run the Conservative Party.
I did not see any standing ovation in Transcona. I do not know anybody that was yearning, that felt punished by the fact that there was not a $500,000 lifetime capital gains exemption.
Check with the member for Humboldt-Lake Centre.

There is no one there who would be in a position to benefit from such a measure. Yet that was the high point for the Conservatives.
The member for Kindersley-Lloydminster brings up the old Conservative bug-a-boo about capital gains with respect to farmland. He knows, as well as I do, that we have always said that that falls into a different category.
How is that different?

But the Conservatives make no distinction between that and flipping condos in Florida, which is regarded by Conservatives as useful economic activity. When humans are at their best is when they are flipping condos in Florida and making money without doing a damn thing. That is what Conservatives live for.
Ordinary folk who are working eight hours a day, nine to five, doing the things that make the world go around, do not count. It is the people who are flipping condos in Florida and making big money. They are the people who have to be protected by capital gains tax exemptions. They are the people who have to be protected so that they can take what they make and put it away in expanded RRSPs. They are the people who have to be protected by the whole tax system. That is why we have a deficit in this country. It is not because of social spending or health care or education. It is because that for too long the whole tax system has been a big scam. The real impact of RRSPs, if you ask me, Mr. Speaker, has been to cut elements of the middle class in on the scam and, in so doing, hopefully silence them about the whole system. The problem with the deficit is tax expenditures, not government spending.
When I was elected in 1979 the Conservatives, under the right hon. member for Yellowhead who had the integrity to live up to one of the promises made by his party, released what was called a tax expenditure account. In that the government did what many people have been requesting for years. They said it is not just a question of taxes collected and money spent. There is also this third element, this unseen element in our
February 14, 1990

finances. It is what money is out there that we could have collected, but we did not what is technically called tax the expenditures.
Mr. Speaker, you remember; you were there. The Conservatives brought out this tax expenditure account, to their credit. The tax expenditure account, if I remember correctly, for that year showed that in that year the Government of Canada forfeited in the form of tax expenditures $32 billion. In that same year the deficit was $14 billion.
In that same year, when people were hysterical about the deficit even then, the fact remained that what the government did not collect in the form of tax expenditures was more than twice the annual deficit. It is not to say that all tax expenditures are wrong. For instance, the child tax credit is not. This is not a blanket condemnation of all tax expenditures.
But we know that many of those tax expenditures have taken the form of various kinds of incentives for business. At that time there was a lot of money being spent in terms of super depletion allowances, depletion allowances, write-offs, you name it, in the north to get oil companies to go around making the Arctic look like a pin cushion. They were getting $1.10 for every dollar that they spent. They could not lose, whether they ever discovered any oil or not.
Those kinds of things continue. A Conservative government might come along and clean up a few things that the Liberals were doing, but with the other hand it would create other opportunities for the corporate community to farm the tax system, to farm the taxpayers' pockets, to farm the pockets of ordinary Canadians so that their position, whether it be individual or corporate, could be enhanced.
What are we faced with? At the same time as the government is enhancing a provision that already costs the government $5 billion to $6 billion a year, ordinary Canadians, like a lot of the CN pensioners in my riding, cannot even get to their cottages any more because they cut the train. Ordinary folk cannot take the train any more because even on the trains that are left the fares have sky-rocketed.
All this is done in the name of fiscal restraint, while with the other hand we need to make life a little easier for those who might have $15,000 to put aside in an RRSP. It makes you want to puke, Mr. Speaker. It
Government Orders
absolutely makes you want to puke when you think about the priorities of this government.
What are we going to see in the budget because the government has to give away more money in the form of RRSPs? We are going to see, we are told but we hope not, cut-backs to Established Programs Financing, transfers to the provinces, which are transferred to the provinces for the financing of health care and post-secondary education. The health care system is already strained to the absolute limit. The federal government is being criminally irresponsible with the medicare system by constantly, budget after budget, unilateral decision after unilateral decision, putting more and more of the burden on to the provinces. At some point the system will break. It will be these same people the government likes to cater to through the tax system who will be the first ones to call for a private health care system alongside the public health care system.
Who will be on the losing end of that? It will be the people who will have to use the public health care system, the people who do not qualify for RRSPs, the people who like to use the trains, the people who are not part of all the frequent flyer clubs with everybody going back and forth to Singapore and everywhere else because they are part of the aircraft culture that leaves people who use trains in a hole somewhere.
They ask what this is all about. It is a totally misguided and immoral direction that this government is taking the whole country in and the middle class, what is left of it, will be eliminated. The upper middle class might survive, but the middle class will be eliminated. We will all be running around cutting each other's throats for jobs that are paying less and less.
The kind of people that this country has been built on-decent, hard working, honest, organized people- who have managed to make a good living because they have strong trade unions and have worked in traditional industries actually producing something, are the people who are on the hit list of this government. These are the people who have to disappear because of international competitiveness and because of the free trade agreement, because of privatization and all of the other things that this government has visited on the Canadian people like an affliction. It is similar to the way the Egyptians were afflicted with the seven plagues. We have been

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
afflicted as a country with the various plagues that this government has brought down on us.
Just the other day I learned that Varda Batteries, a company in Winnipeg, was closed down because Investment Canada approved its purchase by an American company. Five days after the purchase was approved the battery plant shut down. That is what I call real good policy on the part of the Conservative government.
The other day I heard that Air Canada, now privatized, is going to contract out its commissary services, its food service industry. The jobs of 450 people are threatened because Air Canada has to be like everybody else. They have to contract out here, contract out there, and contract our there.
Do you know what it is, Mr. Speaker? It is all just union busting. It is nothing else other than union busting, taking people who have been able to make a decent living because they have been paid a decent wage and putting them in a position where they go from $12 to $6 an hour or $18 to $9 an hour, or whatever the case may be, and that is called progress. We in this party call it despicable.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member mentioned the seven plagues in Egypt. I thought that the Conservative attitude was much more that they expect the taxpayer to be like Job and suffer repeated humiliations.
I want to ask about RRSPs as they relate to capital investment funds. I wonder whether one of the motivations behind this move is not that the Conservatives have been told by their friends in the investment business, particularly those in mutual funds, life insurance, and all those types of financial organizations that are using the pools of RRSP money for their investment purposes, to make sure that there is this pool of investment. The person gets such a great tax benefit from it. It gives all this amount of captured money which can then be spent in investment. This is opposed to what they really should be doing, which is to increase dramatically the contributions to the Canada Assistance Plan. That would, then, give the government a pool of money it could use for capital investments which would benefit all Canadians, not just the ones who had control over pools of capital investment.
I remember talking with a person in the life insurance industry. We were talking about private life insurance programs, many of which are pawned off as pension plans by the private industry, and the business about the Canada Assistance Plan. He said: "They are going to make sure the Canada Assistance Plan is never going to be adequate, because if it is it would mean the death of private pension funds, life insurance programs and that they could not raise the money to liquidate if they had to".
I am wondering if the hon. member has any comments as to how much of this is part of a structure simply to make sure that mutual funds and other life insurance companies, particularly American ones, have an adequate pool of investment capital at their disposal.

Mr. Speaker, what the hon. member points out is that this is part of an ongoing struggle between those who would like to see investment decisions in Canada be part of a larger public decision-making process and those who feel that investment decisions are purely a private matter that should be in the hands of insurance companies or the corporations, or whatever. That is why there is so much resistance to accumulation in the public sector of funds that might actually be used in some intelligent way, according to some rational plan about what the Canadian economy might look like.
They hold to the view that the best form of plan is no plan at all, that all the random individual and corporate decisions are cumulatively the invisible hand of Adam Smith which will look after everyone in the final analysis.
Tell that to the thousands of homeless in Canada. Tell them that Adam Smith's invisible hand has looked after them.
Tell that to the hundreds of thousands of children in this country who are in poverty. Tell them that Adam Smith's invisible hand has looked after them. It has not been an invisible hand; it has been a mailed fist.
One of the things that has always amused me with respect to investment capital is many of the countries which free enterprisers across the way have always held up as examples of economic productivity. I would not want to hold them up that way, because I have other criticisms to make of them.

Take Japan, for instance. One of the reasons it has been as successful as it has is that it has influenced investment, because there has been a political will on the part of government to make collective decisions about investment vis-a-vis a long range plan for the country. What happened in Japan in the last 30 or 40 years was not the result of a whole bunch of individual investment decisions. It was the result of government influencing investment decisions.
In Canada this has always been regarded as Communist or Bolshevik, or whatever. That is why in both Canada and the United States we are going down the tubes economically because we do not have the political will to have an industrial strategy, or even a post-industrial strategy, or any strategy at all like they have in Europe or Japan or in other places. We are going to pay a price for not having that political will.
We have tied ourselves to a falling star called the United States of America, which has even less political will to have such a strategy. Until the people of Canada say to the Canadian government that they want some sort of political accountability for investment decisions, we are going to continue to have the kind of problems we have and the kind of pension system we have.

Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the speech of my hon. friend from Winnipeg-Transcona and hear the more particularized aspect of some of the other things. When I spoke, I spoke on a more broad perspective. I would like to refer briefly to the hon. member's comments about CN pensions and the particularization of that. I note that two members from our party, the member for Burnaby-Kingsway and the member for Nickel Belt have not forgotten, as the government has, about CN pensions and the problems with them. I point out and ask for the comments of my friend as to whether the following motion put forward as Motion No. 427 by the member for Burnaby-Kingsway would do something toward fixing the ills this government has been ignoring in so far as CN pensions are concerned for the last six years. The motion states, in part:
- the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation concerning the pension fund of Canadian National Railway, which:
(l)would provide that pensions be indexed to the extent thatsuch indexation is actuarially viable with the funds that have been paid into the plan, the unfunded liabilities of the company, and the funds that are being paid into the plan on a current basis; and that, in any event, the minimum indexation to be paid should be indexation to
Government Orders
the consumer price index commencing on the retirement date of each pensioner, including those currently receiving pensions; and (2) would provide that excess earnings on money contributed by employees and former employees must be distributed on an equitable basis to employees and further employees only, and not go into corporate coffers.
Would this go some way in assisting my friend?

Mr. Speaker, it certainly would. What the hon. member for Okanagan-Similkameen has outlined, as part of a motion submitted by the hon. member for Burnaby-Kingsway, is precisely the kind of measure that the government should be taking in respect of CN pensioners and also with respect to many other pensioners.
Here we are again talking about people who can take advantage of this expanded RRSP limit. If they have $15,000 a year they can put it in an RRSR Yet all the employees of Route Canada ended up with no pension at all. No pension at all, after some of them having worked 20 years or 30 years, because this government privatized CN Route. It sold it to one of its buddies who turned over some of the assets and made a lot of money in New York somewhere. The people in Transcona and elsewhere in the maritimes who worked for Route Canada were left with absolutely zilch. That is the definition of justice for pensioners that we get from this government.
Looking after pensioners like the people who lost their jobs with Route Canada and looking after the people from CN is the type of action that we need, and it is the kind of action that we have not been getting.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: The time for questions and comments has expired.

Mr. Speaker, I am not pleased to participate in this debate today, but I feel that I must because there is something very sinister going on in this House today.
I have just come from the Standing Committee on Finance where members of the New Democratic Party said that since most Canadians do not understand the details of the proposed goods and services tax and they cannot get answers when they phone the GST hotline, they thought it was appropriate to travel so people could express their views and ask questions about matters which concern them, whether they be ranchers, community groups, native people, small business organizations or simply individuals. It would appear that the committee is going to say no, that it does not want to have any more input into this. Although 80 per cent of the people are opposed to it, the committee says: "That is okay, we are

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
just going to ram it through the House of Commons by ramming it through the committee first".
That exposes what is really going on in here. The government is of the mood that since it has the majority, in terms of the last federal election, it can do anything it wants and it gives them carte blanche to just do whatever it wants, whenever it wants and in whatever way it wants.
Mr. Speaker, you are sitting in the chair today, and government members largely sit on that side of the House and the opposition members sit on this side of the House. It is a balance, and that is our parliamentary system. The government expresses its views on certain pieces of legislation or motions that it puts before the House. The opposition has an obligation and a responsibility to provide an opposition viewpoint to critique legislation or motions in a positive way or, in some cases, to congratulate the government on certain initiatives and vote with the government to send a message out to the people of Canada, such as the message on linguistic duality. We feel strongly about that. I hope that the motion comes before the House tomorrow and we rally around and say that this is something we believe in, that it is important and we unanimously support this motion. What a wonderful message that will send to people who are perhaps wondering where members of the House stand, where certain political parties stand or where certain individuals stand. We will send a clear message.
We could have a whole list of areas where the government has simply said: "Listen, we are the boss. We are big brother. We know what is best. We know what taxes to introduce. The fact that 85 per cent of people do not agree with the goods and services tax, that is okay. We will just ignore that. We are going to use closure, time allocation, cut off debate and curtail debate because we are the government. We can do anything". Well, we are about to see that that is not the case.
I know the government does not think that that can be done. Let me put the government on notice right now that we believe it can. We believe that when the rights of
the opposition are trampled upon and ignored, when the rights of the opposition are simply laughed at by the government, it is going to be in for a major surprise. We will have to wait for a day or two to find out what that surprise is, Mr. Speaker, but I think the government is going to be very surprised that it simply cannot act in this big government way.
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, what this goods and services tax is going to mean. Thousands of new tax collectors are going to be hired, not 10, not 100, not 1,000, but thousands. John Bulloch, the president of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, the person who has studied this legislation from one end to another says that probably, in the end, 25,000 new tax collectors will have to be hired. For every tax collector there will have to be secretaries, researchers, filers, and so on, so we are not talking about 25,000, but maybe 50,00 to 70,000 or more bureaucrats, plus their offices, jet fares, and travel allowances. My goodness.
However, this is not a discussion of the goods and services tax. We are discussing something equally silly. Those people who are watching on television, whose incomes are $85,000 or more annually, are sitting on the edges of their chairs because this legislation is for them.
If you are an ordinary working person, retired person, or a person on an old age or disability pension, this is not for you. This is for an upper income earner in our country. If your income is in the $85,000 bracket, finally you have some good legislation coming your way, because who is going to benefit from this? When you look through the list, the main beneficiary are those folks who are providing for their retirement whose incomes are $86,111.
When I think of all the letters I get from people who are concerned about their pension incomes, I hardly get any letters from people whose incomes are $86,000 plus a year who are worrying about their pension. As a matter of fact, I do not know if I get any letters. I do get a lot of letters from people who are unable to live a dignified life on their existing pensions. I am serious. I get a lot of letters. I am sure all my colleagues in the House get
February 14, 1990

letters from people living in major metropolitan areas whose only income is Canada Pension and the OAS and who just cannot get by. They have to rely on other sources of income, relatives, friends, the food banks or thrift houses just to get by.
What does the government do? Do they bring in increases to the old age security? No, no. Do they bring in an enhanced CPP? No, no. Do they bring in more support for people on veterans' pensions and disability pensions? No, no. They want to help those people whose incomes are $85,000 a year so they can provide for their pensions years.
We have got everything really haywire here. On whose side is the government? This is not pension legislation, it is tax legislation. What this is going to do is enable people to avoid paying income tax now, set aside thousands of dollars and the idea is that they pay it later. Mr. Speaker, you and I know that that is not necessarily the case, because later means that you will be paying it at a much lower rate. Many people, particularly those people whom this legislation is aimed at, will move to a tax haven in their retirement years. They will move to one of the Caribbean Islands where they do not have to pay income tax. They take their money and they do not pay taxes on it there. The old argument that they would eventually pay tax does not hold water. For some, yes, but for many that is not the case.
What does this legislation do for the problems of portability of pensions? Absolutely nothing. What does it do for the 90 per cent of people on private pension plans with no indexation to combat increasing inflation? Absolutely nothing. What does it do to for people who have been waiting years and years for homemakers' pensions? Nothing. There is no mention of homemakers' pensions for those who stay home to care for an ailing family member or relative or a disabled person in their home. There is no concern for those people who need a homemaker's pension. However, for those people watching whose incomes are in excess of $86,000, this is for you. This is the government's pension scheme for you, because presumably those people are in desperate need.
This is going to cost the government millions of dollars. We do not know exactly how many hundreds of millions. What I have here in terms of some of the early
Government Orders
analysis is that somewhere between $300 and $350 million will be lost next year. In other words, these people are not going to pay taxes. If they do not pay then-fair share, we know who is going to be paying more than they should. It is the ordinary working people of the country. The small business people and the farmers will be paying more than they should. This is really a tax dodge in many respects for upper-income people. We are going to lose from the federal treasury about $300 or $350 million a year.
If we are going to wilfully lose that, rather than give it to those whose incomes are in excess of $86,000, it would enable the government to give a $30 a month increase to the 600,000 elderly single women who have no other source of income and who are now living below the poverty line. Is that not interesting? If the government would amend this legislation, we could assist 600,000 elderly single women who are living below the poverty line by giving them an extra $30 a month. Perhaps to many people that does not sound like a lot of money, but for a single elderly woman living below the poverty line an extra $30 a month would go a long way. The government states that we cannot afford that. We cannot afford to consider a homemaker's pension. We cannot afford to look at portability. We have to help these people in the upper income brackets. That is what the Conservative government does.
There is another creeping bit of hypocrisy in this. I remember the Minister of Finance standing up not long ago saying: "Listen, you know those wealthy people who presently get pensions, we should get some of that back. They do not need the pension." So the government introduced legislation that the Minister of Finance called clawback legislation. I thought that was an appropriate name. If you earn a certain income and receive the old age security, the government claws back either all of it or part of it. In other words, the government said that upper income people do not need any pension plans, they can deal with it on their own.
Then along comes Bill C-52 which states that people in the upper income brackets need help, they need to have tax incentives to provide for their retirement years. There seem to be some double standards and a certain amount of speaking out of one side of your mouth one day and the other side another day. There does not seem to be any consistency here, unless the government is

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
trying to fool people into thinking that they are actually doing something worth while.
I have been sitting here for a long time listening to the Conservative members explain one aspect of this legislation. Today, if your income is $20,000 and you want to set aside money to contribute to an RRSP, you can set aside $4,000, if you have the $4,000. However, in 1995 when this legislation kicks in at the most advantageous level, if your income is $20,000 you cannot contribute $4,000. You can contribute only $3,600. In other words, if you earn $20,000 this legislation is going to penalize you in terms of RRSP accessibility. It penalizes people at the low income level, while at the same time at the upper income level one can now contribute $7,500 and in 1995 will be able to contribute $15,500. The lower income earner is going to be penalized by this RSP legislation.
I have been listening carefully to hear from hon. members why the government is doing this and so far I have not heard any reasonable explanation. It puzzles me why we would be making it more difficult for low income people to set aside money via the RRSP programs.
There are whole other sets of reasons here that various researchers have indicated why this is bad legislation. My colleagues before me have explained that at some time, but perhaps I should mention one small thing. I notice my good friend from Toronto is here. He has been a good friend for many years. He gave a very elegant and eloquent speech against this particular initiative. As a matter of fact, it was one of the better speeches I have heard and I applaud him for those remarks.
However, I want to remind my hon. friend that I remember in 1984, and I am sure he does too, that there was a Liberal government at that time. Marc Lalonde was the Minister of Finance. He said that we have to help these upper income people save for their retirement years. We have to bring in changes to the RRSP.
In the Liberals' green paper on pension reform of 1982 they recommended what we are essentially doing here in Bill C-52. In 1984 the Liberal government introduced legislation that was essentially the same as what we have here today. Even my friends opposite on the Conservative benches went on for days and days against this Draconian measure that was helping the most privileged
in the country at the expense of those at the low income level.
At that time the Liberals thought this was great legislation. We have now flipped across the way and the roles are reversed. We now have my hon. friend articulating very well all of the down sides of this legislation and wondering why on earth why the government would do this, and those members now on the government espousing the advantages and the need to help those in the upper income brackets with their pension savings.
I mention as a point of interest more than anything how people can change their views on things whether they are on the opposition benches or the government benches.
Let me summarize by suggesting that this legislation is not going to help many people at all. As a matter of fact, only a certain portion of Canadians take advantage of RRSPs. Today, 20 per cent of Canadians use the RRSP in terms of a method of postponing paying taxes and/or providing money for retirement years later. Naturally, this is largely a result of the tax planning of people in the middle or upper income brackets.
When one looks at the number of people in the veiy low income brackets who file for RRSPs, less than 1 per cent actually file RRSPs, virtually no one. When one gets up into $50,000 and plus incomes, the number of tax filers contributing to RRSPs is nearly 60 per cent. In other words, the overwhelming majority of people in those brackets find that to be a useful way to defer taxes to some time later, if at all.
Let us recognize what we are doing. The government is asking us to pass legislation that will benefit those in the upper income brackets. It will cost the federal government about $350 million a year in lost taxes and this is all happening on the eve of the budget. People are fanning out across the country to try to put a certain spin on the public mindset about what is going to happen. They are saying that the deficit is too large and we must curtail a whole variety of social programs.
One of the toughest days I have had lately was in my hometown of Kamloops. The Y in that community asked the federal government for support to enlarge and expand the women's shelter in our community. There was a long list of people requiring shelter because of various forms of abuse. I do not want to go into the details, but it is a very tragic situation. The government said it was sorry, but it does not have any money, those hundreds of women and those hundreds of families each
February 14, 1990

year will just have to be on their own and find some way to deal with their very serious abuse problems.
All that was sad, Mr. Speaker, but I find it rather odd if you cannot have a few thousand dollars to help a community group establish a women's shelter in the community of Kamloops, and the same argument could be made in many communities across Canada, and in the same breath say that we are prepared to forgo $350 million in income because of the changes to the RSP program to help those people in the upper income brackets. I just find it rather disgusting. If people knew this and understood what is going on, I do not think they would feel good about this at all. This is the kind of thing that makes the people of Canada curious about what this government is doing.
On the one hand it seems to be trying to curtail expenditures and on the other hand providing handouts and financial bonanzas to a very select, privileged few in our society. I guess, without being simplistic, Mr. Speaker, that is what one would expect from the Conservative government. That seems to be the basic theme that one hears whenever there is a Conservative government in office.
In conclusion, there is no question that we have been taxed too much. This last year has seen the thirty-second tax increase initiated by this federal government. In other words, in five short years this government has increased taxes 32 different times with the GST.
When people write to me they say that we cannot take it any longer, we pay so much tax. The government slaps another one on, and 32 tax increases in five years is too much. I just want to make the point that there have been 32 tax increases in the mandate of this government to date. I cannot imagine what the mandate is going to result in if we have another two or three years of this government left. In conclusion, let me say that I am against this RSP legislation.

Mr. Speaker, just a quick comment and a question for my colleague from Kamloops. Ele is probably aware that in response to our allegation that this will cost some $300 or $350 million a year in terms of loss to the public treasury, which could be used in alternate programs, the government has suggested that that is not really accurate. That has not been suggested today because government members are noticeably absent from this debate this afternoon, as is the Official Opposition, but they have said on other occasions that this will be mitigated in part at least by the fact that it will plug up some of the loopholes in the system.
When I heard that I could not help but think of an old Donald Duck or Goofy cartoon that I read when I was just a little tyke about three feet tall. Donald Duck or Goofy was out in a boat on the lake and it had a leak in the bow. He thought he could stop the boat from sinking by chopping a big hole in the stem and letting the water that was coming in in the bow out the aft end, but it did not work. A government that says it is as concerned about deficits as this one is going to find out that chopping another hole in the other end of the boat does not work either.
My colleague may also be aware that Frank Speed, vice-president of the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Association states: "The new tax rales with their pension adjustments and pension adjustment reversals seem likely to be another administrative nightmare that will squeeze more pension plans out of the system."
Also, in May 1988 the joint committee on taxation of the Canadian Bar Association and the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants called the amendments: "Perhaps the most complicated tax rules ever devised."
It seems obvious to me at least that if you are creating that much more gobbledegook and complications around the tax system, with any loopholes you are plugging on the one hand you are probably kicking more holes in the system on the other. My recollection is, and perhaps my colleague from Kamloops will clarify it for me, that this is the same party that said in 1984 and in years before and since that one of their major crusades was to simplify the tax system.

February 14, 1990
Government Orders
The question I want to ask my colleague is in light of both of these, does he think that the members opposite simply do not care about tax simplification? Were they not telling the truth at that time, do they not care about debt reduction or are they just misled?

There are a lot of questions in there, Mr. Speaker, from my hon. friend for Kootenay West-Re-velstoke. Let me begin with his reference to the fact that there were no Conservative members speaking on this RRSP legislation. I am dismayed and a bit disappointed in that because I would have liked to have heard their explanations, particularly because of the fact that those in the $20,000 bracket will actually lose as a result of this legislation in terms of the amount of money they can set aside for their pension years.
I am not surprised, but I do hope when we pick up this debate first thing in the morning that we will hear a number of Conservative members. If nothing else, I can ask them some questions. It is hard to get at the people over there when nobody speaks.
With reference to the complicated tax rules, I tried to make the point that with 4,000 new tax collectors, and perhaps that will be up to 6,000 or 7,000 with all of the other people, it is going to be a red tape nightmare that will descend on this country and on an already over-complicated tax system. This is tax filing time. I sat down to begin the process the other day and got totally depressed. I do not know if anybody has started their tax filing yet. I try to do it without an accountant and I blow it every year. I end up going to the accountants. I just cannot do it myself.
Going back to the question, is the Conservative government serious about deficit reduction? My hon. friend, who is the chairman of the finance committee, was here a moment ago and I see one of his colleagues from Edmonton is with him. Perhaps we can set aside some time in the finance committee to go through all the corporate tax expenditures and evaluate those expenditures on a profit and loss basis to see if we get the financial bang for those bucks that we lose. In those cases where we do, we can even enhance some of those tax exemptions. On the other hand, if we cannot demonstrate clearly that we are not getting good return for that tax loss, then we should shelve the whole thing. We have got to go through that step by step because if we do that, I think people in the country will have a lot more faith in some of the cuts that are being touted by the government.
Until we go through that process, and all the people of Canada know that there are literally billions of dollars, not millions but billions of dollars lost every year to the federal treasury because of corporate tax exemptions and various other exemptions, and I am just talking about the corporate taxes because that is where the big losses are, there will never be support for any tax reform in this country because they know who is going to lose and who is going to gain.
